chapter_summary:
Having grasped the fundamentals of cryptography, our next step as ethical hackers is to understand how these systems are attacked. Cryptographic attacks aren't always about breaking the underlying mathematical algorithms; often, they exploit weaknesses in implementation, key management, or the human element. We will delve into several prominent attack types and explore the powerful tools used to execute them, emphasizing their ethical application for security testing.

screens.title: Cryptographic Attacks and Tools
screens.subtitle: How attackers exploit weaknesses, and how ethical testers use tools to find them

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how attackers approach cryptography from a practical perspective. We will look at several attack types—brute-force, dictionary, rainbow table, and known-plaintext—and why many of these attacks succeed not because math fails but because implementations, keys, or people make systems vulnerable. You will also see how ethical testers responsibly use command-line tools like Hashcat and John the Ripper to simulate attacks and help organizations fix weaknesses. For each technique we’ll cover the core idea, a concrete example, a common misconception to avoid, and one practical defense. By the end you should be able to identify which attack type applies to a scenario, choose an appropriate testing tool, and recommend defensive changes that reduce exposure. Remember, these techniques are for authorized testing only—our goal is to strengthen systems by revealing realistic risks before attackers exploit them. Consider how the human element or poor key management in your environment might be the real path an attacker uses.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Many cryptographic failures arise from weak keys, implementation mistakes, or human choices rather than flawed algorithms. Ethical use of password-cracking tools helps find and fix those gaps before attackers do.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will routinely recognize common cryptographic attack types and explain why they work. You will learn to categorize brute-force, dictionary, rainbow table, and known-plaintext attacks and connect each to the underlying weakness it exploits. You will also gain practical familiarity with Hashcat and John the Ripper as tools for ethical password testing, understanding when and why to use them. Finally, you will be able to recommend concrete mitigations — such as salting hashes, enforcing stronger keys, and improving key management — and explain how these defenses reduce risk. Each objective is tied to an applied milestone: you will analyze a password hash set, choose an appropriate test, and produce a remediation report. These skills matter because detecting weaknesses through authorized testing prevents real attackers from succeeding, and because many failures arise from configuration or human error rather than cryptographic math. As you progress, keep an ethical mindset: scope tests, document consent, and avoid destructive operations unless explicitly permitted.

screens.subtitle: How to demonstrate competency during a penetration test

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on the applied evidence and the testing mindset you must bring. You should be able to select an attack method based on observed artifacts: for example, a list of unsalted password hashes suggests rainbow-table or dictionary-style testing, while short PINs or simple passwords point to brute-force testing. You will also learn how to prepare and document tests: capture authorized scope, choose non-destructive modes when possible, and keep reproducible notes so a team can validate your findings. That conversion from cracking result to operational guidance is the core of ethical testing. This objective ensures you leave with skills you can apply in a real engagement while keeping legal and ethical boundaries clear.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.2 › Learning Objectives — Skills & Evidence

Skills & Evidence

This page emphasizes how you prove competence: correct test selection, safe execution, and clear remediation guidance.

Milestone-focused
Test selection

Match observable artifacts — unsalted hashes, short secrets, or known plaintext — to the optimal attack method. Choosing the right test saves time and reduces risk.

Safe execution

Use non-destructive options, keep backups, and prefer offline testing where possible. Always operate inside a signed scope of engagement.

Documentation

Record the hash type, the method used, sample cracked items, and reproducible steps so others can validate and remediate the issue.

Remediation

Translate results into prioritized fixes such as adding salts, increasing key length, or improving password policy and key rotation.

Practical mnemonic
Observe → Select → Test → Document → Remediate. This sequence keeps testing efficient, ethical, and action-oriented.

screens.title: Attack Surfaces for Cryptography
screens.subtitle: Where attackers find practical ways in without breaking math

narration.text: When we talk about attacking cryptography, it's important to separate math-level breaks from practical attack surfaces. A mathematical break tries to invert an algorithm or find a weakness in the cryptographic primitive; these are rare and often theoretical. Practical attackers focus on easier targets: weak or short keys, poor key management, missing salts, predictable plaintext, or system implementation mistakes. For example, a system that stores password hashes without a salt exposes everyone to precomputed rainbow tables. A second example is using short numeric PINs; brute-force is trivial against four-digit secrets. As an ethical tester you examine these surfaces: look for stored hashes, check whether salts are used, examine password policy and key rotation, and audit who has access to private keys. A common misconception is thinking strong algorithms alone are enough; in practice the surrounding controls matter more. Your task is to map each observed artifact to a likely attack method so you can choose the least invasive, most effective test. Consider this: which would you test first — a set of unsalted hashes or an AES key stored with weak access controls? The right answer usually maximizes evidence while minimizing disruption.

keyIdea.title: Attack surface principle
keyIdea.text: Attackers exploit surrounding weaknesses—key length, salts, storage, or human choices—more often than breaking cryptographic math.

content.html:
Core Concept › Attack Surfaces for Cryptography

Definition and practical examples

Attack surfaces are the parts of a system where an attacker can apply effort to obtain secrets or bypass protections without needing to cryptanalyze algorithms.

Stored hashes without salt
Enables rainbow-table attacks because identical passwords share identical hashes.
Short passwords or PINs
Make brute-force or exhaustive search practical in reasonable time.
Weak key management
Keys stored with overly broad access or in plaintext permit practical key theft.
Key Takeaway

Focus first on accessible, fixable weaknesses around keys and secrets; they are the most common route attackers take.

Supporting explanation

  • Implementation errors and configurations are exploited more often than mathematical flaws.
  • Check whether salts, iteration counts, and key lengths meet modern guidance; absence suggests targeted tests.
  • Human factors—reused passwords, poor rotation, exposed backups—create low-cost attack paths.
Concrete scenario
You find a database dump with password hashes and no salt column. That artifact points you to precomputed table or dictionary-style attacks as a first, low-impact test.
Common misconception
Believing a strong algorithm alone guarantees safety. In reality poor configuration or key handling often undermines strength.

screens.title: Brute-Force Attacks
screens.subtitle: Systematic exhaustive search and when it is practical

narration.text: A brute-force attack tries every possible key or password until it finds the correct one. The method is simple but often limited by the size of the search space. For strong cryptographic keys like long symmetric keys, brute-force is practically infeasible—this is why algorithms with long key lengths remain secure. Yet brute-force is highly effective against short or poorly chosen passwords and PINs. For example, a four-digit numeric PIN has only ten thousand possibilities, which an attacker can test quickly. As an ethical tester, you simulate brute-force where allowed to measure how quickly an account or a device might be compromised and to verify rate-limiting and lockout controls. A typical testing process is: enumerate the target's accepted character sets and length limits, estimate the search space size, run controlled attempts or offline cracking against captured hashes, and report the time-to-compromise and recommended controls. A common mistake is testing online against production accounts without protections; prefer offline hash testing or explicit lab environments. Consider: how would you convince a client to increase complexity or enable throttling based on a measured time-to-compromise?

keyIdea.title: Brute-force practicality
keyIdea.text: Brute-force is a baseline test: trivial for short secrets, impractical for large key spaces. Use it to validate rate limiting and password complexity defenses.

content.html:
Definition › Brute-Force Attacks

How brute-force works

An exhaustive trial of every possible secret until a match is found. The cost is determined by the size of the search space.

Estimate search space
Calculate the number of possible values from length and character set to understand feasibility.
Prefer offline testing
Crack captured hashes in a lab or controlled environment, not against production logins.
Key Takeaway

Use brute-force tests to validate complexity and throttling; for strong keys, focus on other attack surfaces.

Process steps

  1. Define target scope and get authorization.
  2. Gather constraints: length limits and allowed characters.
  3. Estimate search space and decide if offline cracking is needed.
  4. Run controlled attempts and report time-to-compromise and mitigations.
Concrete example
Testing a forgotten device PIN in a lab: if the PIN is four digits, the search space is small and a brute-force simulation shows the need for lockout or biometric fallback.
Common mistake
Running high-volume online brute-force against production logins without throttling or explicit consent; this risks service disruption and ethical violations.

screens.title: Dictionary Attacks
screens.subtitle: Targeted guessing using wordlists and common patterns

narration.text: A dictionary attack uses a curated list of likely passwords instead of trying every possible combination. Wordlists often contain common passwords, leaked credentials, or permutations that reflect human choices—so they can be far more efficient than raw brute-force. As an ethical tester you choose or build wordlists that reflect the target’s likely password patterns: organization-specific terms, common substitutions, or leaked password sets relevant to the industry. Running a dictionary-style test often starts with a fast pass using common lists, then moves to tailored lists and mangling rules that add digits, symbols, or case variations. A critical misconception is assuming dictionary attacks are unsophisticated; in practice, well-crafted wordlist attacks recover many real passwords quickly. Use offline cracking against captured hashes when possible, and always document the wordlist and rules used so your results are reproducible. The evidence you present should show which items were cracked and why they were likely chosen by real users, leading to targeted policy changes such as banned-password lists and improved user training. Dictionary Attacks means well-targeted wordlists and mangling rules are more effective than blind brute force against human-chosen passwords; they reveal realistic risk fast.. In practical terms, targeted guessing using wordlists and common patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dictionary efficiency
keyIdea.text: Well-targeted wordlists and mangling rules are more effective than blind brute force against human-chosen passwords; they reveal realistic risk fast.

content.html:
Core Concept › Dictionary Attacks

What a dictionary attack is

A targeted sequence of guesses derived from wordlists and known patterns to prioritize likely secrets instead of trying every possibility.

Wordlist selection
Start with common lists, then add organization-specific or leaked-password samples to reflect realistic user behavior.
Mangling rules
Apply rules that append numbers, swap letters, or change case to increase coverage without exploding the search space.
Key Takeaway

Tailor wordlists to the target to find user-chosen secrets quickly and create focused remediation like banned lists or training.

Supporting explanation

  • Commonly used wordlists can recover many real-world passwords in minutes when applied to captured hashes.
  • Applying mangling rules increases success while remaining efficient compared to blind brute-force.
  • Document list provenance and rules so findings are reproducible and explainable to stakeholders.
Concrete example
Using a wordlist that includes the company name and common variants often recovers reused or company-themed passwords during a corporate engagement.
Common misconception
Assuming dictionary attacks are amateurish; well-built lists and rules are a professional tester's fastest way to find realistic vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Rainbow Table Attacks
screens.subtitle: Precomputed hash maps and why salts matter

narration.text: A rainbow table is a precomputed mapping from plaintext passwords to their hashed values. Attackers build these tables ahead of time so that, when they obtain a hash, they can quickly look up the corresponding plaintext. This technique is extremely fast against unsalted hashes because identical passwords produce identical hashes. The primary defense is to use a unique salt per password: salts change the input to the hash function so precomputed maps no longer apply. Another important nuance is that rainbow tables work best against simple hash algorithms and short passwords; strong hash functions with iteration and salt greatly reduce the utility of precomputation. Ethical testers should check whether salts and iterations are used, and if they are absent, demonstrate the risk by attempting offline lookups on a small sample in a controlled environment. A common mistake is thinking salting alone is sufficient; salts must be unique and paired with strong hashing parameters to be effective. Your recommendation should be to add per-password salts, use a slow hash function or key derivation function, and avoid storing raw or predictable secrets.

keyIdea.title: Rainbow vs salted hashes
keyIdea.text: Precomputed maps defeat unsalted hashes quickly. Unique salts and slow hashing render rainbow tables ineffective.

content.html:
Comparison › Rainbow Table Attacks

How rainbow tables work

Precompute plaintext-to-hash mappings so lookups are fast when a target hash is obtained. Effective only when salts are missing and hashes use fast algorithms.

Precomputation tradeoff
Tables are large to build but allow rapid cracking later. Salts break the approach by altering inputs.
Defenses
Per-password salts plus a slow hash function or key-derivation function remove rainbow table advantages.
Key Takeaway

If hashes lack unique salts and appropriate hashing parameters, precomputed attacks become a real and fast threat.

Side-by-side

Unsalted hash
Same plaintext → identical hashes. Rainbow tables can quickly reveal the plaintext.
Salted hash
Unique salt per entry breaks direct lookup; attacker must compute per-salt tables, which is expensive.
Concrete example
A database with a single hash column and no salt is a red flag: show a controlled demonstration on one entry to illustrate the exposure and recommend per-password salts immediately.

screens.title: Known-Plaintext Attacks
screens.subtitle: When attackers use known input to reveal key-dependent behavior

narration.text: A known-plaintext attack relies on the attacker having both some plaintext and the corresponding ciphertext. With that pair, the attacker studies how the cipher transforms input and may be able to deduce information about the key or identify implementation weaknesses. In real-world ethical testing, the known-plaintext scenario often appears when predictable messages are encrypted in a repeatable way, or when file headers or protocol fields are constant and reveal patterns. It's important to note that known-plaintext attacks are not always practical against modern, properly implemented ciphers, but they can reveal weak modes of operation, poor use of IVs, or reuse of keys across contexts. As an ethical tester, you should look for repeated encrypted structures, reuse of initial vectors, or encryption with predictable prefixes. A common misconception is to assume known-plaintext instantly breaks the algorithm; in practice, it reveals implementation patterns that allow targeted testing. Finish by documenting evidence and recommending safer modes, per-message initialization, and proper key separation. Known-Plaintext Attacks means known plaintext helps reveal implementation weaknesses or key reuse, not necessarily a direct mathematical break of modern ciphers.. In practical terms, when attackers use known input to reveal key-dependent behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Known-plaintext insight
keyIdea.text: Known plaintext helps reveal implementation weaknesses or key reuse, not necessarily a direct mathematical break of modern ciphers.

content.html:
Core Concept › Known-Plaintext Attacks

Definition and why it matters

When an attacker has both plaintext and ciphertext, they can observe how encryption behaves and look for weaknesses such as key reuse or predictable IVs.

Where it appears
Protocols with static headers, predictable messages, or reused keys across files frequently provide known-plaintext opportunities.
Tester actions
Identify repeated encrypted structures, check IV usage, and test whether keys are reused across contexts.
Key Takeaway

Known plaintext is most useful to detect bad implementation or reuse patterns; recommend per-message randomization and key separation.

Supporting explanation

  • Modern ciphers resist simple known-plaintext breaks, but implementation issues can leak information.
  • Look for reused IVs, deterministic encryption, or key reuse across different data classes.
  • Document the pattern, illustrate with small non-production samples, and recommend randomized IVs and strong key management.
Concrete scenario
A backup archive uses the same key and IV for many files. This reuse reveals structural patterns across ciphertexts and suggests a direct remediation: use unique IVs and rotate keys.

screens.title: Password-Cracking Tools Overview
screens.subtitle: What Hashcat and John the Ripper provide for ethical testers

narration.text: Hashcat and John the Ripper are two widely used command-line tools for offline password cracking. They provide flexible engines for brute-force, dictionary, and hybrid attacks and support many hash formats. As ethical testers we use them to simulate realistic attacks against captured hash sets in a controlled environment. Hashcat is often chosen for G P U-accelerated cracking when speed is needed; John provides a versatile, scriptable approach and built-in formats for many systems. When preparing a test, choose the tool based on the hash type, available hardware, and the rules you want to apply. Document which hash format you tested, the wordlist and rules used, and whether the run was G P U or C P U-based. Importantly, do not run these tools against live authentication endpoints without explicit permission. A common misconception is that tool choice alone determines success; in practice the right wordlist, rule set, and correct hash identification matter more. Your deliverable should show example outputs, methodology, and a recommended next step such as forcing password resets or adding salts and iterations. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tool selection
keyIdea.text: Choose Hashcat or John based on hash format, hardware, and desired attack rules; document methodology and avoid testing live endpoints without permission.

content.html:
Definition › Password-Cracking Tools Overview

What these tools do

Provide engines for offline attacks: brute-force, dictionary, hybrid, and rule-based transformations across many hash formats.

Hash identification
Identify the hash type before testing so you can select the correct attack mode and prevent wasted effort.
Document hardware
Note whether GPU acceleration was used; performance affects your time-to-compromise estimates and recommendations.
Key Takeaway

Tools are enablers; success depends on correct format identification, sane wordlists, and ethical execution within scope.

Concrete example snippets

Below are conceptual examples showing the kinds of configurations you document when you run a controlled test. These are descriptive and intended for reporting, not step-by-step execution.
# Example: report entry (conceptual)
# Hash format: bcrypt
# Tool: John the Ripper
# Wordlist: corporate-banned.txt + leaked-sets
# Hardware: CPU-only
# Result: 12/10,000 hashes cracked in initial pass

# Example: report entry (conceptual)
# Hash format: unsalted-md5
# Tool: Hashcat (GPU)
# Wordlist: common-passwords.txt
# Rules: append-digit, l33t-substitutions
# Result: many matches via precomputed and rule-based runs
Ethical reminder
Only run offline cracking with explicit authorization and never target live authentication endpoints unless the scope allows it.

screens.title: Preparing an Ethical Crack Test
screens.subtitle: A reproducible checklist and sample workflow

narration.text: Preparation is central to ethical password cracking. Start by confirming written authorization and scope limits; know which systems and data sets you can test. Next, capture a representative, minimized sample of hashes rather than entire production datasets; this reduces risk and preserves privacy. Identify the hash format so you can select appropriate tools and modes. Choose your wordlists and rules deliberately: begin with common lists, then apply targeted lists that reflect the client’s context. Decide whether the test will be C P U or G P U-based and record hardware. Run tests offline in a controlled environment and log the exact commands, wordlists, and rules so results are reproducible. After cracking, produce a findings section that contains sample evidence, the method used, the estimated time-to-compromise, and priority remediation steps. A common misconception is that a single run proves everything; multiple passes with different lists and rules often reveal additional compromised secrets. Your artifact should be a concise reproducible lab notebook entry the client can verify, not raw tool output dumped without context. Preparing an Ethical Crack Test means document scope, sample selection, hash identification, wordlist choices, hardware, and results so findings are verifiable and actionable.. In practical terms, a reproducible checklist and sample workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reproducible workflow
keyIdea.text: Document scope, sample selection, hash identification, wordlist choices, hardware, and results so findings are verifiable and actionable.

content.html:
Process Flow › Preparing an Ethical Crack Test

Step-by-step checklist

  1. Obtain signed authorization and define scope and exclusions.
  2. Select a minimized sample of hashes for testing and protect privacy.
  3. Identify hash formats and required tool modes.
  4. Choose wordlists and mangling rules; record provenance.
  5. Decide hardware mode (CPU/GPU) and prepare a controlled lab environment.
  6. Log all commands, options, and outputs that support your findings.
Pro tip

Keep sample sets small and representative to reduce risk and speed up reproducible testing.

Concrete example report entry

# Report excerpt (conceptual)
Scope: offline test of 200-sample hashes from user DB (consent obtained)
Hash type: unsalted SHA-1 (identified via header)
Tool: Hashcat - GPU
Wordlists: common-10k.txt + org-names.txt
Rules: append-digit, capitalization
Results: 18/200 cracked in first pass
Remediation: add per-password salt; migrate to slow KDF; require stronger password policy
Common mistake
Publishing raw tool output without context. Always include methodology, samples, and recommended remediation so stakeholders can act.

screens.title: Example: Ethical Use of Hashcat (Conceptual)
screens.subtitle: Documentation and reporting—what to capture and why

narration.text: When you use Hashcat in an authorized lab, your purpose is to create reproducible evidence rather than to brute-force everything indiscriminately. Capture the following: the hash format you tested, the exact input sample and how it was anonymized, the wordlists and any transformation rules applied, and hardware details such as G P U model. If a run succeeds, include representative sample output that ties a cracked hash back to a test entry, not a full dump. In the report, estimate time-to-compromise under the used hardware profile and explain how additional defenses—salting, stronger hashing parameters, or rate-limiting—would change that estimate. Avoid operational detail that could enable misuse: provide enough information for remediation but not a turnkey recipe for exploitation beyond the authorized scope. A misconception to correct is thinking that fast cracking proves the algorithm is broken; rather, it shows the secret was too weak or stored improperly. Close with a prioritized remediation list and a test plan for the client to validate fixes after changes are applied. Example: Ethical Use of Hashcat (Conceptual) means provide reproducible evidence, contextualized time-to-compromise, and prioritized mitigations—avoid over-sharing operational details that could be misused.. In practical terms, documentation and reporting—what to capture and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Report with restraint
keyIdea.text: Provide reproducible evidence, contextualized time-to-compromise, and prioritized mitigations—avoid over-sharing operational details that could be misused.

content.html:
Process Flow › Example: Ethical Use of Hashcat (Conceptual)

What to capture for a report

  • Hash format identification and how it was determined.
  • Sample selection and anonymization approach.
  • Wordlists, mangling rules, and their provenance.
  • Hardware profile and runtime estimates.
Key Takeaway

Reports should enable remediation and validation without creating an actionable playbook for misuse outside the authorized context.

Conceptual example entry

# Lab note (conceptual)
Sample: 50 anonymized hashes from dev DB
Hash type: unsalted SHA-1 (identified by header)
Tool: Hashcat (GPU)
Wordlists: common-100k + org-derived list
Rules: capitalization + append-year
Result: 7/50 cracked; estimated additional time for 80% coverage on current hardware: 3 days
Recommended fixes: add unique salts, migrate to slow KDF, enforce stronger policies
Common misconception
Publishing exhaustive technical steps in a report can increase risk. Provide enough to act, and plan a re-test to verify fixes instead.

screens.title: Implementation & Human Weaknesses
screens.subtitle: Why good cryptography fails in practice

narration.text: Strong algorithms are necessary but not sufficient. Implementation mistakes, key management failures, and human behavior are the usual causes when cryptography fails. Examples include storing keys with overly broad access, failing to rotate keys, omitting per-entry salts, or allowing weak user-chosen passwords. Humans often reuse passwords across systems, so a crack in one environment can cascade into many accounts. Implementation mistakes like deterministic encryption, reused IVs, or wrong modes of operation undermine protections even when the algorithm itself is sound. As an ethical tester you look beyond the algorithm: check configuration, access controls, and operational practices such as backup and key distribution. Remediation often focuses on process: introduce key rotation policies, tighten access to key material, require salted and iterated hashes, and enforce stronger password policies with technical controls. A misconception is to think that changing the cipher alone fixes the issue; instead, changing surrounding practices and storage models usually yields the best security improvement. Finish by prioritizing fixes that reduce attack surface with the least operational friction. Implementation & Human Weaknesses means failures usually come from implementation, keys, and people. fix the processes around cryptography as the highest-impact defense.. In practical terms, why good cryptography fails in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical failure modes
keyIdea.text: Failures usually come from implementation, keys, and people. Fix the processes around cryptography as the highest-impact defense.

content.html:
Comparison › Implementation & Human Weaknesses

Common real-world failures

  • Keys stored with broad access or in plain files instead of secure stores.
  • Absence of per-entry salts or weak hashing parameters for stored secrets.
  • Password reuse and weak policies that make dictionary attacks practical.
Key Takeaway

Attack the people and process problems first: improving storage, rotation, and access control typically reduces the most risk.

Remediation checklist

Use per-password salts and slow KDFs
Salts and iterations slow offline attacks and prevent precomputation.
Control key access and rotate keys
Limit who can read key material and rotate keys so exposed keys have limited lifetime.
Harden password policies and technical controls
Banned lists, complexity, and rate-limiting reduce success of offline and online guessing.
Common misconception
Switching ciphers without changing storage or access controls often leaves the system as vulnerable as before.

screens.title: Defenses and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Concrete mitigations to reduce cryptographic attack risk

narration.text: Defenses start with proper storage and operational discipline. Always use per-entry, unique salts for stored secrets and employ a slow key derivation function or password hashing algorithm to increase attacker cost. Enforce strong password policies and banned-password lists to reduce predictable, user-chosen secrets. Add rate-limiting and account lockouts for online authentication to raise the cost of brute-force attacks, and monitor for repeated failed attempts. For key material, use secure key storage, minimize privileged access, and rotate keys periodically so exposures are time-limited. During testing and reporting, recommend prioritized changes: first apply low-effort, high-impact fixes like salting and banning common passwords; next tighten key access and rotation; finally, evaluate migrating to stronger algorithms or re-encrypting legacy data as needed. A typical misconception is thinking all changes must be cryptographic; operational controls like throttling and training often yield immediate protection. Close with a plan to re-test after fixes so the client can validate the reduction in time-to-compromise and residual risk. Defenses and Best Practices means start with salts and slow kdfs, enforce password policy and throttling, then improve key management and re-test to validate risk reduction.. In practical terms, concrete mitigations to reduce cryptographic attack risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Start with salts and slow KDFs, enforce password policy and throttling, then improve key management and re-test to validate risk reduction.

content.html:
Process Flow › Defenses and Best Practices

Immediate, high-impact actions

  • Implement unique per-password salts and migrate to a slow KDF for stored secrets.
  • Enforce banned-password lists and stronger complexity rules to reduce human-chosen weaknesses.
  • Apply rate-limiting, multi-factor, and lockout policies to online authentication.
Key Takeaway

Start with fixes that increase attacker cost dramatically while minimizing user disruption, then follow with process and key-management improvements.

Longer-term controls

Secure key storage
Use hardware modules or managed key stores and limit access to key material.
Key rotation and separation
Rotate keys on an operational schedule and separate keys by purpose to reduce blast radius.
Re-testing plan
Schedule a re-test after remediation to confirm reduced time-to-compromise and residual exposures.
Common misconception
Thinking only cryptographic algorithm changes are needed. Process and storage changes usually have larger and quicker effect.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders of the most important ideas

narration.text: Let's recap the essential ideas you must carry forward. First, attackers usually exploit weaknesses around cryptography—weak keys, poor storage, missing salts, or human choices—rather than breaking algorithms. Second, choose your testing method to match the artifact: brute-force against short secrets, dictionary and wordlists against user-chosen passwords, and rainbow-table checks only when salts are absent. Third, Hashcat and John the Ripper are powerful tools for offline, authorized tests; success depends more on correct format identification and wordlists than on tool choice alone. Finally, prioritize defenses that raise attacker cost quickly: unique salts, slow key derivation, rate-limiting, and stronger key management. When you report, provide reproducible evidence, explain time-to-compromise, and recommend prioritized, practical fixes. These steps ensure ethical testing helps organizations reduce real risk without creating new vulnerabilities. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to use in tests and reports

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders in every engagement. First, identify artifacts and map them to likely attack methods—this chooses a focused, low-impact test. Second, use Hashcat or John in offline, authorized conditions and record your wordlists, rules, and hardware so results are reproducible. Third, prioritize fixes that increase attacker cost dramatically with minimal operational impact: salts, slow hashing, access controls, rotation, and throttling. Use this checklist to keep testing ethical, efficient, and action-oriented. What to Remember › Quick Reference
Map artifacts
Choose attacks by what you observe, not by a guess of math-level failure.
Document tests
Save format, lists, rules, and hardware for reproducibility and remediation validation.

Salts, slow KDFs, throttling, and key management reduce practical attacker success quickly.
Final takeaway
Ethical cryptographic testing is about revealing operational weaknesses and enabling prioritized fixes. Use the right method, document it, and help your client reduce real-world attack success.
